etymology: The descendants of Israel, the name God gave Jacob at Peniel — a prince with God, one who has power with God and with men. The Authorized Version uses Israelites where it wishes to name the people as individuals rather than the nation, and Paul uses it for the covenant privileges he grieves over in Romans 9.
biblical_def: Israelites names the covenant people one by one. Even in Egypt, before there is a nation in any political sense, the plagues distinguish them: there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead (Exodus 9:7). The law binds the feast of tabernacles on them by birth — all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths (Leviticus 23:42) — a yearly week under branches to remember that their fathers had no house. In the Gospels the word becomes a commendation from the lips of Christ Himself: Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile! (John 1:47), spoken of Nathanael, and the contrast with Jacob, whose name meant supplanter and whose life was full of guile until Peniel, is surely intended. Paul lists the privileges of the name in the passage where he says he could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen: Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises (Romans 9:4). Then he makes the distinction the whole chapter turns on: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel. The name is real, the privileges are real, and neither is salvation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ISRAELITE as a descendant of Israel or Jacob; a Jew. The 1828 entry treats the word as simply ethnic, which is exactly the assumption Romans 9 dismantles by distinguishing Israel after the flesh from the Israel of God.
webster_full: ISRAELITE, n. — A descendant of Israel or Jacob; a Jew.
The name Israel was given at Peniel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed (Genesis 32:28).
The Authorized Version uses children of Israel for the nation in its corporate acts and Israelites where individuals are in view.
Paul’s three-fold challenge in 2 Corinthians 11:22 — Hebrews, Israelites, the seed of Abraham — shows the terms were distinguishable to a first-century ear.
Webster’s plain ethnic definition is correct as far as English goes; Scripture’s own usage carries a covenantal freight no dictionary entry can supply.
scriptures: Exodus 9:7
And Pharaoh sent, and, behold, there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.
Leviticus 23:42
Ye shall dwell in booths seven days; all that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths:
John 1:47
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!
Romans 9:4
Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;
2 Corinthians 11:22
Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? so am I.
corruption_summary: Two errors divide the field: dispensationalism, which keeps Israel and the church permanently separate with two programmes and two peoples, and the replacement caricature that treats the promises as simply cancelled. Romans 9 through 11 refuses both.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s method in Romans 9 is to grant every privilege and then deny that privilege saves. Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants — he does not minimize one item. Then: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel, and he proves it from Isaac against Ishmael and Jacob against Esau, both cases of natural descent that did not carry election. Dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession, keeps the two peoples on separate tracks with separate destinies and thereby loses the one olive tree of Romans 11, into which believing Gentiles are grafted and from which unbelieving branches are broken off. There is one tree. There always was.

The opposite error, and the one the dispensationalist rightly fears, is a triumphalism that speaks of the church as though God had simply finished with Israel. Romans 11 forbids it in terms: Hath God cast away his people? God forbid, and boast not against the branches, and be not highminded, but fear. The Reformed position has room for a large ingathering of Jews — the Puritans expected one, and the Westminster divines prayed for it — without inventing a second programme of redemption. What it will not do is make ethnic descent a saving category, because he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly, and the Israelite indeed is the one in whom is no guile.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yisra’el (H3478), he will rule as God, or one who strives with God, from sarah to contend and El, God; Greek Israelites (G2475).
roots_lines: Hebrew Yisra’el (H3478) — Israel; given at Peniel (Genesis 32:28) and confirmed at Bethel (Genesis 35:10).
Hebrew sarah (H8280) — to contend, to have power as a prince; the verb in as a prince hast thou power with God.
Hebrew Yaaqob (H3290) — Jacob; heel-catcher, supplanter — the name replaced, and the guile John 1:47 says Nathanael lacks.
Greek Israelites (G2475) — an Israelite; John 1:47, Romans 9:4, 11:1, 2 Corinthians 11:22.
Greek dolos (G1388) — guile, deceit, bait; in whom is no guile (John 1:47).
usage: All that are Israelites born shall dwell in booths (Leviticus 23:42) — a week each year under branches, to remember.
Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile (John 1:47) — Christ’s commendation, and the reversal of Jacob.
Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption (Romans 9:4) — every privilege granted, and none of them saving.

etymology: The people of Asshur, the second son of Shem (Genesis 10:22) and the city and land named for him on the upper Tigris. Webster 1828 defines ASSYRIAN as pertaining to Assyria. In Isaiah the Assyrian is the great instrument of God’s anger and the great case study in how God judges the instrument He uses.
biblical_def: The Assyrians are the empire God chose as His rod, and Isaiah 10 is the definitive passage on what that means. O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation. I will send him against an hypocritical nation… to take the spoil, and to take the prey (Isaiah 10:5-6). The commission is explicit, and then comes the qualification that makes the passage a permanent theological landmark: Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few (Isaiah 10:7). Assyria intends conquest; God intends chastening; and Assyria’s intention is what Assyria will answer for — I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria (Isaiah 10:12). They took Samaria and carried the ten tribes away (2 Kings 17:6). They came against Hezekiah and Rabshakeh mocked the God of Israel from the wall, and the answer came in one night: the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand (Isaiah 37:36). And Isaiah 19 ends with the astonishing promise of a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and God calling Assyria the work of my hands.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ASSYRIAN as pertaining to Assyria, and as a noun, a native of Assyria; the older gazetteers place the kingdom on the Tigris with Nineveh as its capital, which is exactly the geography of Jonah and Nahum.
webster_full: ASSYRIAN, a. — Pertaining to Assyria, an ancient kingdom of Asia, on the Tigris.
ASSYRIAN, n. — A native or inhabitant of Assyria.
The name is from Asshur, the second son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), and from the ancient city of Asshur on the Tigris.
Nineveh, their capital, is the city of Jonah’s preaching and of Nahum’s burden; that great city of Jonah 4:11.
Webster’s brief entry gives geography; Isaiah, Jonah, and Nahum give the theology of the empire.
scriptures: Isaiah 10:5
O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation.
Isaiah 10:7
Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few.
Isaiah 10:12

Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks.
2 Kings 17:6
In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.
Isaiah 37:36
Then the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 10:5-12 is the clearest statement in Scripture of the compatibility of divine sovereignty with human guilt, and it is the passage most often avoided by those who insist the two cannot stand together.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arminian objection and the open-theist objection both assume that if God ordains an act, the agent cannot be culpable for it. Isaiah 10 states both halves without apology and without explanation. God sends the Assyrian, gives him a charge, and calls him the rod of His anger; the Assyrian does not mean it so, intends conquest and glory for himself, and is punished for the stout heart with which he did precisely what God sent him to do. The Reformed doctrine of concurrence is the attempt to say no more and no less than this text says. God ordains the act; the creature performs it freely, according to his own nature and intention; the intention is the creature’s own and is judged as such. Joseph’s brothers, Pharaoh, Assyria, and Acts 2:23 on the crucifixion all stand or fall together.

The second corruption is the assumption that being used by God is evidence of God’s favour. Assyria was the rod, and Assyria was broken. Nebuchadnezzar is called my servant and Babylon is destroyed. Judas fulfilled the scripture and it had been good for that man if he had not been born. Whole ministries, movements, and nations have been the instruments of real good and have perished; God’s use of a man says nothing about that man’s standing. Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? The one thing Assyria could not do was mistake usefulness for salvation, and neither can anyone else.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ashshur (H804), Asshur, both the man (Genesis 10:22) and the land; the gentilic is Ashshuri; Nineveh is Nineweh (H5210).
roots_lines: Hebrew Ashshur (H804) — Asshur, Assyria; the son of Shem and the empire named from him.
Hebrew shebet (H7626) — a rod, staff, sceptre, tribe; the rod of mine anger (Isaiah 10:5).
Hebrew matteh (H4294) — a staff; the parallel term in the same verse.
Hebrew Nineweh (H5210) — Nineveh, the capital; the city spared under Jonah and destroyed under Nahum.
Hebrew Rabshaqeh (H7262) — Rabshakeh, the title of the Assyrian officer who blasphemed from the wall (2 Kings 18:19).
usage: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger (Isaiah 10:5) — the empire named as God’s own instrument.
Howbeit he meaneth not so (Isaiah 10:7) — the distinction that preserves both sovereignty and guilt.
The angel of the LORD… smote in the camp of the Assyrians (Isaiah 37:36) — the rod broken in a night.

etymology: The people of Babylon, Hebrew Babel, confusion — the city of Genesis 11 and the empire of Nebuchadnezzar. Ezekiel calls them the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their nativity. From Genesis to Revelation, Babylon is Scripture’s standing name for the city of man set against the city of God.
biblical_def: The Babylonians are the Chaldean empire that took Jerusalem, burned the temple, and carried Judah into the seventy years. God names them as His own instrument in language even more startling than He uses of Assyria: I will send and take all the families of the north… and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant (Jeremiah 25:9). Habakkuk could not stomach it and said so in the great prophetic complaint, and God’s answer begins, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation (Habakkuk 1:6). Daniel opens with the fact stated flatly and with the theology in the next verse — the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand. Ezekiel uses them in his most searing indictment of Judah’s political adultery: the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love (Ezekiel 23:17), the alliance Judah courted becoming the power that destroyed her. And to the exiles already in that city Jeremiah wrote the letter that has governed Christian civic life ever since: build houses, plant gardens, take wives, and seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives (Jeremiah 29:7). Revelation ends the account: Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BABYLONIAN as pertaining to Babylon, and BABYLONISH as pertaining to Babylon, or, figuratively, mixed and confused — a sense taken from the confusion of tongues at Babel and carried into Reformation polemic against Rome.
webster_full: BABYLONIAN, a. — Pertaining to Babylon, the ancient city on the Euphrates, or to the empire of which it was the capital.
BABYLONIAN, n. — An inhabitant of Babylonia; also, in the older writers, an astrologer, from the reputation of the Chaldean star-gazers.
BABYLONISH, a. — Pertaining to Babylon; also mixed, confused — from the confusion of tongues at Babel (Genesis 11:9).
A goodly Babylonish garment was part of Achan’s spoil at Jericho (Joshua 7:21), the first plunder to destroy an Israelite household.
Webster’s second sense records the Reformation habit, following Revelation 17-18, of calling any corrupt religious system a Babylon.
scriptures: Jeremiah 25:9

Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the LORD, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations.
Habakkuk 1:6
For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs.
Ezekiel 23:17
And the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their whoredom, and she was polluted with them, and her mind was alienated from them.
Jeremiah 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Revelation 18:2

And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 29 is quarried for a single verse about God’s plans while the letter it belongs to — a command to settle down under a pagan tyranny for seventy years and pray for its welfare — is passed over entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you is printed on graduation cards and coffee mugs as a promise of personal prosperity. It was written to a deported people, four verses after they were told to build houses and plant gardens in the land of their captors, and the thoughts of peace God knew toward them were to be realized after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon — that is, after nearly everyone reading the letter was dead. Jeremiah had to add a warning against the prophets among them who were promising a quick return, because that is always the more popular message. The verse is a real promise; it is a promise to a covenant people about a corporate future beyond the lifetime of most who received it, and lifting it out of that is not encouragement but flattery.

The letter’s actual instruction is the more valuable thing, and it is the charter of Christian citizenship under a government that is not Christian. Seek the peace of the city; pray for it; in its peace you shall have peace. That is written of Babylon, the city that had just burned the temple, and it is the same instinct as Paul’s command to pray for kings and all in authority under Nero. It rules out both the withdrawal that treats the surrounding city as no concern of ours and the revolutionary impulse that treats it as the enemy to be overthrown. Daniel served in that administration at the highest level and would not eat the king’s meat or stop praying at his window. That is the pattern: full civic engagement, absolute religious refusal.
roots_summary: Hebrew Babel (H894), Babylon, connected in Genesis 11:9 with balal, to confound; Kasdim (H3778) is the Chaldeans; Greek Babylon (G897).
roots_lines: Hebrew Babel (H894) — Babel, Babylon; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9).
Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mix, to confound; the wordplay behind the name.
Hebrew Kasdim (H3778) — Chaldeans; the ruling stock of the Babylonian empire (Habakkuk 1:6).
Hebrew Nebukadretstsar (H5019) — Nebuchadnezzar, also spelled Nebuchadrezzar; called my servant at Jeremiah 25:9.
Greek Babylon (G897) — Babylon; the great harlot city of Revelation 17-18 and, most take it, Peter’s cipher in 1 Peter 5:13.
usage: Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant (Jeremiah 25:9) — a pagan tyrant given the covenant title of servant.
Seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away (Jeremiah 29:7) — the charter of exile citizenship.
Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen (Revelation 18:2) — the end of the city of man.

etymology: Hebrew Anaqim, the descendants of Anak, whose name is connected with the word for a neck-chain or collar — the long-necked. They held Hebron and the hill country of Judah, and their reputation is what turned Israel back at Kadeshbarnea for forty years.
biblical_def: The Anakims are the giants of Hebron, and they are the measure by which every other tall people in Scripture is described — the Emims, the Zamzummims, and the Rephaim are all reckoned as the Anakims. The ten spies made them the whole substance of their report: there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight (Numbers 13:33). That last clause is the fatal one, since no spy could possibly know how he looked to a giant; the report had already passed from observation into imagination. Forty years later Moses names the fear honestly and answers it: A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak! (Deuteronomy 9:2) — and then, Understand therefore this day, that the LORD thy God is he which goeth over before thee. Caleb, at eighty-five, asked for the very mountain the spies had feared: thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there… if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out (Joshua 14:12). He drove them out. There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained (Joshua 11:22) — and Gath afterward produced Goliath.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no ANAKIM entry. The Hebrew plural is retained by the King James translators, as with Emims and Rephaims; the root is generally connected with a neck-chain, hence the traditional gloss long-necked.
webster_full: ANAKIMS, n. pl. — The descendants of Anak; a race of tall men who inhabited Hebron and the hill country of southern Canaan.
The name is usually derived from Hebrew anaq, a necklace or collar, whence the sense of long-necked or of those who wore the ornaments of chiefs.
Arba, from whom Hebron was formerly called Kirjatharba, was a great man among the Anakims (Joshua 14:15).
Three sons of Anak are named at Numbers 13:22 — Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai — and Caleb drove out all three (Joshua 15:14).
The survivors at Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (Joshua 11:22) supply the background to Goliath of Gath and his brethren.
scriptures: Numbers 13:33
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
Deuteronomy 9:2
A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak!
Joshua 11:22
There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained.
Joshua 14:12

Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day; for thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced: if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out, as the LORD said.
Joshua 14:15
And the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba; which Arba was a great man among the Anakims. And the land had rest from war.
corruption_summary: Numbers 13:33 has been made the proof text of Christian self-esteem teaching — the idea that Israel failed because they thought too little of themselves. The text says they failed because they thought too little of God, and the grasshopper line is the report’s clearest evidence of unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight. Preachers regularly treat the first clause as the sin and prescribe a higher self-image as the cure. Read the second clause: they claim to know how they appeared to the giants, which is information no spy possessed. Unbelief is not merely fearful; it is inventive, and it fills in the enemy’s opinion for him. The remedy Scripture actually gives is nowhere in the neighbourhood of self-image. Caleb and Joshua saw the same giants and the same walls and said, the LORD is with us: fear them not. Moses, rehearsing it forty years on, does not tell Israel they are stronger than they think; he tells them the LORD goeth over before them as a consuming fire. The size of the Anakim was never in dispute. The size of God was.

The second thing to mark is Caleb’s request. At eighty-five he asked for Hebron specifically because the Anakim were there and the cities were great and fenced, and he hedged it with the humblest possible clause — if so be the LORD will be with me. That is not bravado; it is faith that names the difficulty accurately and then names God accurately. The generation that refused the mountain died in the wilderness; the man who asked for it at eighty-five got it, and the land had rest from war. Forty-five years of waiting on a promise did not diminish him, because he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel.
roots_summary: Hebrew Anaq (H6061), Anak, and Anaqim (H6062), the Anakims; connected with anaq (H6059), to encircle the neck, hence a necklace or collar.
roots_lines: Hebrew Anaq (H6061) — Anak; the man from whom the clan is named (Numbers 13:22).
Hebrew Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakims; Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 9:2, Joshua 11:21-22.
Hebrew anaq (H6059) — to put about the neck, to adorn with a chain; the likely root of the name.
Hebrew Nephilim (H5303) — giants; the word rendered giants in Numbers 13:33 and Genesis 6:4.
Hebrew Qiryath Arba — Kirjatharba, the city of Arba, Hebron’s older name (Joshua 14:15).
usage: We were in our own sight as grasshoppers (Numbers 13:33) — the report that cost a generation the land.
Who can stand before the children of Anak! (Deuteronomy 9:2) — Moses quoting the fear back before answering it.
Now therefore give me this mountain (Joshua 14:12) — Caleb asking at eighty-five for the giants’ country.

etymology: A body of foreign soldiers forming David’s personal guard, always named with the Cherethites. The names are commonly connected with the Philistines and the Cretans — men from the coast David had lived among in exile, who became the king’s most trusted troops and the only force that stayed loyal through two rebellions.
biblical_def: The Pelethites appear only in company with the Cherethites, and always in the same office: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18), a note repeated at 2 Samuel 20:23 and 1 Chronicles 18:17. They are the royal bodyguard, foreigners in an Israelite army, and their record is remarkable. On the day David fled Jerusalem before Absalom, all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king (2 Samuel 15:18) — the household troops went out with a king who had lost his capital, while Israel’s own counsellor Ahithophel went over to the usurper. When Sheba the son of Bichri raised the second revolt, there went out after him Joab’s men, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men (2 Samuel 20:7). And at the end, when Adonijah had proclaimed himself king, it was Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and Pelethites who brought Solomon down to Gihon and set him on the throne (1 Kings 1:38). Three crises of the house of David, and the foreign guard is on the right side of all three.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no PELETHITE entry. The word appears seven times in Scripture and never alone; its meaning is disputed, but the office — the king’s personal guard under Benaiah — is perfectly clear from the contexts.
webster_full: PELETHITES, n. pl. — A company of David’s guard, always mentioned with the Cherethites, and commanded by Benaiah the son of Jehoiada.
The name is often connected with the Hebrew for Philistine, as Cherethite is with Crete; both would then denote coastland mercenaries.
They are named seven times, all in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings 1, and 1 Chronicles 18 — and never separately from the Cherethites.
An alternative older explanation derives the two names from words for executioners and couriers, the two functions of a royal guard.
Webster 1828 does not carry the term; the office is defined by 2 Samuel 8:18, 15:18, 20:7, 20:23, and 1 Kings 1:38.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 8:18
And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David’s sons were chief rulers.
2 Samuel 15:18
And all his servants passed on beside him; and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king.
2 Samuel 20:7
And there went out after him Joab’s men, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men: and they went out of Jerusalem, to pursue after Sheba the son of Bichri.
2 Samuel 20:23
Now Joab was over all the host of Israel: and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites:
1 Chronicles 18:17
And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covenant loyalty is not produced by blood or nationality, and that the men nearest a king in his fall are rarely the men who have most to gain.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What deserves recovery is the pattern of loyalty in 2 Samuel 15. David goes up the ascent of Olivet weeping, barefoot, his head covered, while the hearts of the men of Israel go after Absalom. Who stays? A guard of Cherethites and Pelethites, six hundred Gittites newly come from Gath under Ittai, Zadok and Abiathar with the ark, and Hushai the Archite. Almost none of them are men with a natural stake in the house of David. Ahithophel, who had every stake, defected. The pattern recurs whenever a good work is under pressure, and any pastor who has watched a church go through a hard season will recognize it: the people who stay are frequently not the ones the register would have predicted.

The second point is a matter of order rather than sentiment. These were foreigners, and they were placed under an Israelite captain, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, who was himself a priest’s son and one of the three mighty men. They are never given command; they are given a charge under authority. Scripture consistently welcomes the stranger into the service of the covenant people while keeping the offices ordered, and both halves of that are needed. A body that cannot receive outsiders becomes a clan; a body that receives them without order becomes something other than itself. David did both rightly, and on the day his own son took his throne it was the foreigners under Benaiah who brought Solomon to Gihon.
roots_summary: Hebrew Pelethi (H6432), Pelethite, always paired with Kerethi (H3774), Cherethite; both names are usually traced to the coastland peoples of Philistia and Crete.
roots_lines: Hebrew Pelethi (H6432) — Pelethite; a courier or runner, on one derivation, from a root meaning to be swift.
Hebrew Kerethi (H3774) — Cherethite; connected with Crete, and used in parallel with Philistines at Zephaniah 2:5.
Hebrew Pelishti (H6430) — Philistine; the likely cognate behind Pelethi.
Hebrew Benayahu (H1141) — Benaiah, the LORD hath built; their captain, and afterward Solomon’s commander-in-chief.
Hebrew mishmereth — a charge, a watch; the standing term for a guard’s appointed duty.
usage: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18) — the guard under an Israelite captain.
All the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites… passed on before the king (2 Samuel 15:18) — loyalty on the day of flight.
Benaiah… was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites (2 Samuel 20:23) — the office kept through both rebellions.

etymology: The people of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom on the east of the sea of Galilee under Mount Hermon, and also a people of the southern desert toward the Philistine border. The Authorized Version uses one English form for both; they are distinct peoples, and the northern one supplied David with a wife and Absalom with a refuge.
biblical_def: The Geshurites are one of the peoples Israel never removed. Joshua’s survey of the unconquered land is blunt: the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day (Joshua 13:13). Their border is named twice in the allotment of Bashan (Joshua 12:5; 13:11), which is to say that the land was described as given while the people on it were left in place. The consequence came through the house of David. Among David’s wives at Hebron was Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, and her son was Absalom. When Absalom had murdered his brother Amnon, he fled to his mother’s people and stayed three years in Geshur, and the unremoved kingdom on the northern frontier became the safe house for a fratricide and the base from which the rebellion eventually came. A southern people of the same name appears in David’s exile raids from Ziklag. The whole account is a single lesson repeated: what Israel tolerated on her border eventually married into her palace.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no GESHURITE entry. Geshur is a place-name meaning bridge, and the Authorized Version uses the gentilic of two distinct peoples — a northern Aramean kingdom and a southern desert clan.
webster_full: GESHURITES, n. pl. — The inhabitants of Geshur, a small kingdom east of the sea of Galilee under Hermon; also a people of the south toward the Philistine border.
The Hebrew Geshur is generally taken to mean a bridge.
The northern Geshur was ruled by Talmai, whose daughter Maacah bore Absalom to David (2 Samuel 3:3).
Absalom fled thither after killing Amnon and remained three years (2 Samuel 13:37-38).
The southern Geshurites appear in David’s Ziklag raids (1 Samuel 27:8) and are a distinct people bearing the same name.
scriptures: Joshua 12:5
And reigned in mount Hermon, and in Salcah, and in all Bashan, unto the border of the Geshurites and the Maachathites, and half Gilead, the border of Sihon king of Heshbon.
Joshua 13:11
And Gilead, and the border of the Geshurites and Maachathites, and all mount Hermon, and all Bashan unto Salcah;
Joshua 13:13
Nevertheless the children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day.
Judges 3:5
And the children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, and Amorites, and Perizzites, and Hivites, and Jebusites:
Deuteronomy 7:2
And when the LORD thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discipline of Deuteronomy 7:2 — that intermarriage with what God commanded to be removed is how a tolerated compromise reaches the throne room in two generations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Joshua 13:13 records a failure in a single clause, and the Chronicler of Israel’s decline never has to mention Geshur again for the reader to see what came of it. David, king in Hebron, married the daughter of the king of that unremoved country, and Absalom was the child of that alliance. Absalom murdered his brother and fled to his grandfather’s court, was sheltered there three years, came back, stole the hearts of the men of Israel, and drove his father barefoot out of Jerusalem. Every step is ordinary politics; the whole chain rests on a border left uncleared. Compromise is rarely dramatic at the moment it is made, and it does not usually harm the man who made it. It harms his grandchildren.

The application to the church is neither about ethnicity nor about literal warfare, and it must be stated carefully or it will be misused. The New Testament’s parallel is unmistakable: be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers, and Paul’s counsel that a widow is free to marry only in the Lord. The line is drawn at faith, never at blood — Rahab and Ruth are in the genealogy of Christ, and the church has always received converts of every nation. What Deuteronomy 7 forbids and 2 Corinthians 6 repeats is covenantal alliance with what remains unconverted, and the Geshurites are the case study in what such an alliance produces given enough time.
roots_summary: Hebrew Geshur (H1650), a bridge; Geshuri (H1651), Geshurite; Maakathi (H4602), Maachathite, their standing companion in the lists.
roots_lines: Hebrew Geshur (H1650) — Geshur; a bridge, the Aramean kingdom under Hermon.
Hebrew Geshuri (H1651) — Geshurite; used of both the northern and the southern people.
Hebrew Maakathi (H4602) — Maachathite; the neighbouring people always named with them in Joshua.
Hebrew Talmai (H8526) — Talmai, king of Geshur; Absalom’s grandfather (2 Samuel 3:3; 13:37).
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to dispossess; the verb Joshua 13:13 says Israel did not perform.
usage: The children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites (Joshua 13:13) — a failure recorded in one clause.
Unto the border of the Geshurites and the Maachathites (Joshua 12:5) — land described as given while its people remained.
Thou shalt make no covenant with them (Deuteronomy 7:2) — the command that would have prevented the whole account.

etymology: Hebrew Yishma’el, God shall hear, named by the angel before his birth: because the LORD hath heard thy affliction (Genesis 16:11). Abraham’s firstborn by Hagar the Egyptian, circumcised in his father’s house, blessed with twelve princes, and passed over for the covenant.
biblical_def: Ishmael is Abraham’s son by the bondwoman, born of a scheme to help God keep His promise. His name is a permanent record of mercy — God shall hear — and the name is honoured twice: once at his conception, when the angel found Hagar by the fountain in the wilderness, and again when Hagar wept over the dying boy in the wilderness of Beersheba and God heard the voice of the lad (Genesis 21:17). Abraham loved him. When God announced Sarah’s son, the old man’s prayer was, O that Ishmael might live before thee! (Genesis 17:18), and God’s answer granted everything except the covenant: as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him… twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation (Genesis 17:20), but my covenant will I establish with Isaac. He was circumcised at thirteen, the first man in history to bear the sign; he lived a hundred and thirty-seven years; and he stood with Isaac at the cave of Machpelah to bury their father (Genesis 25:9). The angel’s prophecy of his temper — a wild man; his hand will be against every man — came true of his descendants. Paul makes him the type of the flesh, born after the flesh, contrasted with the son born by promise.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no ISHMAEL entry as a proper noun, but the English word Ishmaelite had already acquired its proverbial sense of an outcast or one whose hand is against every man — taken directly from Genesis 16:12.
webster_full: ISHMAEL, n. — The son of Abraham by Hagar the Egyptian; the father of the twelve princes of the northern Arabian desert.
The name means God shall hear, and the marginal note of the Authorized Version at Genesis 16:11 gives it so.
He was circumcised at thirteen (Genesis 17:25), and the Arab custom of circumcising at that age has long been traced to him.
Genesis 25:13-16 names his twelve sons, twelve princes according to their nations, exactly as promised at Genesis 17:20.
A later Ishmael, the son of Nethaniah, murdered Gedaliah after the fall of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 41) and is an entirely different man.
scriptures: Genesis 16:11
And the angel of the LORD said unto her, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.
Genesis 17:18
And Abraham said unto God, O that Ishmael might live before thee!
Genesis 21:17
And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.
Genesis 25:9
And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre;
Genesis 25:17
And these are the years of the life of Ishmael, an hundred and thirty and seven years: and he gave up the ghost and died; and was gathered unto his people.
corruption_summary: Ishmael is the standing refutation of the belief that God’s temporal kindness tracks His covenant election — and the standing refutation of the counter-error that those outside the covenant are outside God’s care.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul settles the doctrinal use of the narrative in Galatians 4 and Romans 9. Ishmael was born after the flesh and Isaac by promise; these are two covenants, and the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman. Every part of the older brother’s position was genuinely advantaged: Abraham’s blood, Abraham’s household, Abraham’s circumcision, and Abraham’s explicit prayer offered for him by name. And the inheritance passed the other way, announced before Isaac was conceived. This is unconditional election stated in narrative before it is stated in propositions, and it is the reason no man may reason from his upbringing, his baptism, his family, or his religious advantages to his standing before God.

The opposite error is to read Ishmael as reprobate, which the text never says. God heard the boy’s cry, opened Hagar’s eyes to the well, was with the lad as he grew, gave him twelve princes and a great nation, and answered Abraham’s prayer for him in so many words — as for Ishmael, I have heard thee. Common grace is real, abundant, and undeserved, and it is not saving. The Reformed tradition has always held both, and the pastoral value of holding both is considerable: it prevents a believer from despising the prosperity of the unconverted and from resting in his own.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yishma’el (H3458), God shall hear, from shama (H8085) to hear and El, God; his mother is Hagar (H1904), and his sons are the twelve princes of Genesis 25.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yishma’el (H3458) — Ishmael; God shall hear (Genesis 16:11).
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, to hearken, to obey; the verb in his name and in Genesis 21:17.
Hebrew pere adam — a wild man, literally a wild ass of a man (Genesis 16:12).
Hebrew nasi (H5387) — a prince, a chief; twelve princes shall he beget (Genesis 17:20).
Greek kata sarka — after the flesh; Paul’s description of his birth in Galatians 4:23, over against di epangelias, by promise.
usage: O that Ishmael might live before thee! (Genesis 17:18) — a father’s prayer, answered and yet not granted the covenant.
God heard the voice of the lad where he is (Genesis 21:17) — the name made good in the wilderness.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him (Genesis 25:9) — the two brothers at Machpelah.

etymology: Egyptian, generally understood as he whom Ra has given. Described in Genesis 39:1 as an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian — the commander of the royal bodyguard and keeper of the state prison. He is to be distinguished from Potipherah, priest of On, whose daughter Asenath Joseph married.
biblical_def: Potiphar is the Egyptian officer who bought Joseph from the Ishmeelites and, without knowing it, became the first stage of the providence that saved his own nation from famine. The narrative is careful about the sequence. Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand (Genesis 39:4), and the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Then came Potiphar’s wife, day after day, and Joseph’s answer, which is one of the great sentences of Scripture on the nature of sin: There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God? (Genesis 39:9). He names the wrong against his master and then names it as sin against God, which is where sin’s real weight lies. Potiphar believed his wife, and Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound (Genesis 39:20). The punishment is worth noting: a slave who had actually assaulted his master’s wife would have been executed. Potiphar put him in the prison he himself administered, which is precisely where Joseph needed to be to meet Pharaoh’s butler.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no POTIPHAR entry. The title given him in the Authorized Version, captain of the guard, renders a Hebrew phrase meaning chief of the slaughterers or executioners — the officer over the royal bodyguard and the state prison.
webster_full: POTIPHAR, n. — An officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, who bought Joseph of the Ishmeelites (Genesis 37:36; 39:1).
The Hebrew title sar hattabbachim means chief of the slaughterers, that is, of the executioners or bodyguard; the same title is given to Nebuzaradan under Babylon (2 Kings 25:8).
The prison into which Joseph was cast was under Potiphar’s own authority (Genesis 40:3), which is how Joseph came to serve Pharaoh’s butler and baker.
Potipherah, priest of On, whose daughter Asenath Joseph married (Genesis 41:45), is a different man with a similar name.
The name is Egyptian and is usually read as he whom Ra has given, of the same pattern as Theodore in Greek.
scriptures: Genesis 39:1
And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.
Genesis 39:4
And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.
Genesis 39:9
There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?
Genesis 39:20
And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.
Genesis 41:45
And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphnathpaaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On. And Joseph went out over all the land of Egypt.
corruption_summary: Genesis 39:9 is the text that decides whether a man understands sin at all — and the therapeutic age, which treats wrongdoing as damage to relationships and to the self, has almost no way of hearing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Joseph gives two reasons and puts them in a deliberate order. The first is the wrong against Potiphar, who had withheld nothing from him but his wife; the second, and the one he ends on, is that it would be sin against God. David says the same after a worse fall: Against thee, thee only, have I sinned — not because Uriah was uninjured but because the offence against God is the offence that defines the act. Where sin is redefined as harm, the whole account changes: a private arrangement that harms no one becomes permissible, and repentance becomes an apology to the injured party. Scripture’s definition is a transgression of the law of God, and it is what makes chastity possible in a room where nobody would ever know.

The second thing worth naming is the shape of the providence, which is unbearable while it is happening. Joseph did the right thing at real cost and went to prison for it, and the chapter that records it says four times that the LORD was with him. He was in that prison for years, forgotten by the butler. It ended in a throne, a nation preserved, and the sentence that governs the whole book: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. That is the doctrine of providence stated by a man who had every human ground for bitterness and did not take one of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew Potiphar (H6318), from the Egyptian; the title is sar hattabbachim, chief of the executioners or bodyguard; Potiphera (H6319) is the distinct priest of On.
roots_lines: Hebrew Potiphar (H6318) — Potiphar; from an Egyptian name usually read he whom Ra has given.
Hebrew sar (H8269) — a chief, prince, captain; the first element of his title.
Hebrew tabbach (H2876) — a slaughterer, a cook, an executioner; hence captain of the guard.
Hebrew Potiphera (H6319) — Potipherah, priest of On and father of Asenath (Genesis 41:45); a different man.
Hebrew beth hassohar — the round house, the prison of Genesis 39:20, an expression used only in the Joseph narrative.
usage: Captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him (Genesis 39:1) — the purchase that began the deliverance of a nation.
All that he had he put into his hand (Genesis 39:4) — a heathen house blessed for a believer’s sake.
How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God? (Genesis 39:9) — the definition of sin in a single question.

etymology: Hebrew Tsipporah, a little bird or sparrow, from tsippor, a bird. One of the seven daughters of Jethro priest of Midian, she became Moses’ wife at the well, and it was her hand that performed the circumcision that saved his life on the way back to Egypt.
biblical_def: Zipporah is the Midianite wife of Moses, given him by Jethro after he drove off the shepherds at the well: Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter (Exodus 2:21). She bore him Gershom and Eliezer. The passage that fixes her place in Scripture is the strangest in the book. On the road back to Egypt, at the inn, the LORD met him, and sought to kill him — Moses, going to demand that Pharaoh release God’s covenant son, had not put the covenant sign on his own. Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me (Exodus 4:25), and the LORD let him go. She acted, and her words show she did not like it; obedience is recorded, not enthusiasm. Afterward Moses sent her back to her father, and Jethro brought her and the two sons to the camp at Sinai (Exodus 18:2). The one other reference to Moses’ wife is Numbers 12, where Miriam and Aaron spoke against him because of the Ethiopian woman he had married — and God struck Miriam leprous, defending His servant’s marriage without qualification.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no ZIPPORAH entry. The Hebrew means a bird, the feminine of tsippor, the ordinary word for a small bird throughout the Old Testament.
webster_full: ZIPPORAH, n. — The daughter of Jethro (Reuel) priest of Midian, and the wife of Moses (Exodus 2:21).
The name is Hebrew for a bird or sparrow; the masculine tsippor appears in Leviticus 14 of the birds used in the cleansing of the leper.
Her sons were Gershom, a stranger here (Exodus 2:22), and Eliezer, the God of my father was mine help (Exodus 18:4).
Exodus 4:24-26 is one of the most difficult passages in the Pentateuch, and Zipporah is its acting figure.
Whether the Ethiopian woman of Numbers 12:1 is Zipporah under another description or a second wife has been debated since the fathers; the text does not settle it.
scriptures: Exodus 2:21
And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.
Exodus 4:25
Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me.
Exodus 18:2
Then Jethro, Moses’ father in law, took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her back,
Numbers 12:1
And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman.
Genesis 17:14
And the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people; he hath broken my covenant.
corruption_summary: Exodus 4:24-26 is skipped in almost every retelling of Moses’ life, and the omission removes the sharpest lesson in the Pentateuch about a leader’s household — that God will not send a man to demand covenant obedience of others while he neglects the covenant sign in his own house.
corruption_paragraphs: God had just told Moses to say to Pharaoh, Israel is my son, even my firstborn… let my son go, that he may serve me. On the road, at the inn, the LORD sought to kill him, and the remedy Zipporah applied identifies the offence exactly: a son of Abraham in Moses’ own tent was uncircumcised, in plain breach of Genesis 17:14. The mediator of the covenant was going to prosecute a covenant claim against Egypt with the covenant broken in his own household. The application to the ministry is direct and is made explicit in 1 Timothy 3: a man who does not rule his own house well cannot take care of the church of God. The passage is skipped because it is severe, and it is severe because the office is.

Zipporah herself deserves better than she usually gets. She is often read as resentful, and her words — a bloody husband art thou to me — are certainly not pious. But she is the one who understood what was required, took the flint, and did it, at an hour when her husband was apparently unable. Scripture repeatedly records obedience rendered without warm feeling and does not despise it; the son who said I will not and afterward repented and went is the one who did his father’s will. A Christian wife holding a household to the covenant when her husband has let it slip is doing what Zipporah did at the inn, and it saved Moses’ life.
roots_summary: Hebrew Tsipporah (H6855), a bird, feminine of tsippor (H6833); her father is Yithro (H3503), Jethro, also called Reuel.
roots_lines: Hebrew Tsipporah (H6855) — Zipporah; a little bird, a sparrow.
Hebrew tsippor (H6833) — a bird; the common noun, used of the sparrow alone upon the housetop (Psalm 102:7).
Hebrew tsor (H6864) — a flint, a sharp stone; the instrument she used (Exodus 4:25).
Hebrew chathan damim — a bridegroom of blood; the phrase the Authorized Version renders a bloody husband.
Hebrew Gereshom (H1647) — Gershom; for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land (Exodus 2:22).
usage: He gave Moses Zipporah his daughter (Exodus 2:21) — the marriage made in Midian exile.
Then Zipporah took a sharp stone (Exodus 4:25) — the wife who did what the mediator had not.
Because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married (Numbers 12:1) — the marriage God defended against Miriam.

etymology: Hebrew Betsal’el, in the shadow of God, from tsel, a shadow, and El, God. Son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah — the master craftsman of the tabernacle, and the first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God.
biblical_def: Bezaleel is the first person in the Bible of whom it is written that God filled him with His Spirit, and the filling was for craftsmanship. See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah: And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship (Exodus 31:2-3). The list that follows is a trade inventory — to devise cunning works, to work in gold and silver and brass, in the cutting of stones, in the carving of timber. Moses repeats the whole announcement publicly to the congregation (Exodus 35:30-31), so that Israel should know the appointment was God’s and not the leader’s. With Aholiab of the tribe of Dan and every wise hearted man, Bezaleel and Aholiab… wrought all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the LORD had commanded (Exodus 36:1). And the record closes with the phrase that governs the whole enterprise: Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD commanded Moses (Exodus 38:22). Not what he devised, not what he preferred — all that the LORD commanded. The brasen altar he made was still standing before the tabernacle in Solomon’s day (2 Chronicles 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no BEZALEEL entry. The name means in the shadow of God, and the shadow of God in Hebrew usage is His protection — he that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
webster_full: BEZALEEL, n. — The son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; the chief artificer of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:2).
The name signifies in the shadow of God, from tsel, a shadow, with the divine name El.
His grandfather Hur held up Moses’ hands with Aaron at Rephidim (Exodus 17:12), so the family had already served the LORD conspicuously.
Aholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, was given him as partner and as a teacher of others (Exodus 35:34).
Exodus 31:3 is the first occurrence in Scripture of a man being filled with the Spirit of God, and the gift named is skill in workmanship.
scriptures: Exodus 31:2
See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah:
Exodus 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Exodus 35:31
And he hath filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship;
Exodus 36:1

Then wrought Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whom the LORD put wisdom and understanding to know how to work all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the LORD had commanded.
Exodus 38:22
And Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD commanded Moses.
corruption_summary: Bezaleel is claimed by two opposite parties — charismatic writers who make him a proof text for anointed creativity unbound by form, and a philistine strain of conservatism that treats beauty in worship as a luxury. Exodus refutes both from the same verses.
corruption_paragraphs: The first misuse takes Exodus 31:3 as warrant for artistic freedom in worship: the Spirit fills the artist, therefore the artist’s vision is Spirit-led. But every account of Bezaleel’s work ends with the same clause — according to all that the LORD had commanded, made all that the LORD commanded Moses. He had been given the pattern shewed to Moses in the mount, down to the loops and the taches, and the Spirit filled him to execute it, not to improve it. That is the regulative principle applied to the arts of worship. The gift was extraordinary and the liberty was nil, and the two facts sit in the same sentence without any sense of strain.

The opposite error is the assumption that God cares about doctrine and not about craft. Exodus devotes more chapters to the tabernacle’s construction than to the creation of the world, names the craftsman and his father and his grandfather and his tribe, records that God called him by name, and says the Spirit of God filled him for the cutting of stones and the carving of timber. Blue, purple, scarlet, fine twined linen, beaten gold, engraved onyx — God specified all of it. A congregation that treats beauty as frivolous has not got a higher view of Scripture than one that does not; it has simply not read Exodus 31 with the same attention it gives to Exodus 20.
roots_summary: Hebrew Betsal’el (H1212), in the shadow of God, from tsel (H6738), shadow, and El; his partner is Oholi’ab (H171), the father’s tent.
roots_lines: Hebrew Betsal’el (H1212) — Bezaleel; in the shadow, that is under the protection, of God.
Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow, shade, protection; under the shadow of the Almighty (Psalm 91:1).
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; in Exodus 31:3 it plainly includes practical skill, as it does in Proverbs.
Hebrew melakah (H4399) — work, workmanship, craft; the word behind all manner of workmanship.
Hebrew Oholi’ab (H171) — Aholiab, tent of the father; his partner, of the tribe of Dan (Exodus 31:6).
usage: I have called by name Bezaleel (Exodus 31:2) — a craftsman chosen by God personally and publicly.
I have filled him with the spirit of God… in all manner of workmanship (Exodus 31:3) — the first filling recorded in Scripture.
Made all that the LORD commanded Moses (Exodus 38:22) — extraordinary gift, exact obedience.
